key_terms.meaning: Split of fuel energy into brake power, heat to coolant, heat to exhaust and other losses; typically about 25–30% brake power, 30% coolant, 35% exhaust
Thin extended surface on an air-cooled cylinder or head that adds area for heat transfer to air by convection
Passages cast into the block and head around cylinders, valves and spark plug through which coolant flows
Natural circulation loop: hot, less dense coolant rises from the jacket to the radiator and cooler, denser coolant returns to the bottom of the jacket
A pump, usually centrifugal and belt driven, pushes coolant round the loop at a flow set by engine speed and thermostat opening
Spring-loaded radiator cap that seals the system and holds it above atmospheric pressure, raising the boiling point of the coolant (roughly 3 °C per 10 kPa for water)
Fluid that carries heat from the jacket to the radiator: water plus ethylene glycol for a lower freezing point and a higher boiling point, plus corrosion and scale inhibitors
FP = IP − BP, the power spent on rubbing surfaces and on driving pumps, fans and the valve train
Oil is stored in a pan at the bottom of the crankcase, drawn by a pump, filtered, fed to the bearings and drains back by gravity
Oil drains to a shallow pan, is scavenged to a separate tank and then pumped under pressure to the bearings; allows a low, flat engine and steady supply under cornering
Oil is mixed with petrol in a fixed ratio (often 1:50) for small two-strokes and lubricates every surface as the mixture passes through the crankcase
A number that shows how little an oil's viscosity changes with temperature; a higher VI means a flatter viscosity–temperature curve
Zinc dialkyldithiophosphate, an anti-wear and anti-oxidant additive that forms a protective film on rubbing metal surfaces
A compressor driven mechanically from the crankshaft by belt, gear or chain that raises the density of the air entering the engine
Gauge pressure of the intake air above atmospheric, for example 0.5 bar boost; boost ratio = p₂/p₁ absolute
An exhaust-gas turbine on one shaft with a centrifugal compressor; the turbine uses waste exhaust energy to drive the compressor
Delay between opening the throttle and getting full boost, caused by the time taken to build exhaust energy and spin the turbo up to speed
A turbo with movable vanes at the turbine inlet that close at low gas flow to keep gas speed high, and open at high flow to limit boost
A heat exchanger between the compressor and the intake manifold that cools compressed air, so its density and the trapped air mass rise
Replacing burnt gas in the cylinder with fresh charge in a two-stroke, driven by crankcase pressure or a separate blower through ports placed on the cylinder wall

takeaways: Only about a quarter to a third of the fuel energy leaves an engine as brake power; the rest must be taken away as heat by coolant, oil and exhaust.
Cooling must be controlled, not maximised: too little causes knock, pre-ignition and oil breakdown, while too much raises friction, wear and deposits and lowers efficiency.
Liquid cooling ranges from a thermosyphon loop with no pump to a pressurised pump-driven system, and pressure is the cheapest way to lift the safe upper temperature.
Friction power is a near-fixed tax on indicated power, so clean oil at the right pressure and the right viscosity returns real brake power.
A lubricant is selected by its viscosity grade, viscosity index and additive package, not by how thick it feels between the fingers.
Supercharging raises the air mass trapped per cycle, so a smaller engine can make the same power, at the cost of higher thermal and mechanical loading.
A turbocharger runs on exhaust energy that would otherwise be wasted, so it is more efficient than a belt-driven blower, but that energy arrives late — that delay is turbo lag.
Variable geometry and intercooling attack the turbo's weaknesses from two sides: the vanes fix low-speed boost, the intercooler recovers the density lost to compressor heating.
In a two-stroke the port layout decides how much fresh charge stays in the cylinder; uniflow and loop scavenging lose far less charge than simple cross-flow.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are usually 'explain with a neat sketch' questions — cooling system layout, lubrication circuit, blower or turbocharger working, and the effects of boosting on engine performance.

bank.q: Draw the heat balance of a petrol engine and explain why cooling is necessary. State what happens if the engine is overcooled.
outline: Typical split: 25–30% brake power, about 30% to coolant, about 35% out with exhaust, rest friction and radiation
Overheating effects: knock and pre-ignition, loss of volumetric efficiency, oil thinning and oxidation, thermal stress and warping of the head
Overcooling effects: higher friction and wear, poor fuel vaporisation, sludge and acid formation, lower thermal efficiency
Conclusion: cooling is a control problem, the jacket temperature must be held within a band

bank.q: Compare air cooling and liquid cooling of IC engines with sketches, giving advantages, disadvantages and typical applications.
outline: Air cooling: fins on barrel and head, direct convection, no radiator or pump; needs a fan and ducting on multicylinder engines; local hot spots
Liquid cooling: water jacket, radiator, pump, thermostat, fan; uniform temperature, quieter, compact bore spacing
Comparison table on weight, cost, maintenance, cooling uniformity, warm-up, freezing risk
Applications: air for scooters, motorcycles, small gensets and aircraft; liquid for cars, trucks, tractors and large stationary engines

bank.q: Explain the thermosyphon, forced circulation and pressure cooling systems. Why do modern engines use pressurised forced circulation?
outline: Thermosyphon: density difference drives flow, no pump, needs tall radiator, flow depends on temperature difference, slow warm-up circulation
Forced circulation: pump output, thermostat control, bypass during warm-up, higher flow and smaller radiator
Pressure cooling: sealed cap raises boiling point, about 3 °C per 10 kPa, so a higher jacket temperature is allowed with a smaller radiator and less fan power
Why: stable flow at all speeds, smaller and lighter radiator, no boiling at high altitude or high load

bank.q: Explain the functions of engine lubrication and describe wet sump, dry sump and mist lubrication systems with sketches.
outline: Functions: reduce friction and wear, carry away heat, remove wear debris, seal piston rings, cushion shock loads, resist corrosion
Wet sump: strainer, gear pump, relief valve, filter, main gallery, drillings to mains, big ends, camshaft; oil returns by gravity
Dry sump: scavenge pump, remote tank, pressure pump; advantages in racing, aircraft and off-road vehicles
Mist: oil mixed with fuel, no pump or filter, total loss, used in small two-strokes

bank.q: Discuss the properties required of a lubricating oil and the additives used to obtain them.
outline: Viscosity and its SAE grade; viscosity index and multigrade oils
Pour point, flash point, fire point, cloud point, oiliness, film strength, volatility
Chemical stability: oxidation resistance, resistance to sludge and varnish
Additives: anti-wear (ZDDP), detergent and dispersant, anti-oxidant, pour-point depressant, VI improver, anti-foam, corrosion inhibitor, friction modifier
Why base oil alone cannot meet all requirements

bank.q: A four-stroke engine of 1.5 litre swept volume runs at 3000 rpm and gives indicated power 55 kW against brake power 40 kW. Find the friction power, the mechanical efficiency and the friction mean effective pressure.
outline: FP = IP − BP = 15 kW
Mechanical efficiency = BP/IP = 40/55 = 72.7%
Cycles per second = (3000/60)/2 = 25
fmep = FP/(V_s × cycles per second) = 15000/(0.0015 × 25) = 4 × 10⁵ Pa = 4 bar
Comment on how fmep varies with speed and oil viscosity

bank.q: In a test, 30% of the fuel energy goes to the coolant. Fuel flow is 5 kg/h of calorific value 44 MJ/kg and the coolant water rises 8 °C. Find the coolant flow required in kg/s.
outline: Heat to coolant = 0.30 × 5 × 44000 kJ/h = 66000 kJ/h
Convert to kW: 66000/3600 = 18.3 kW
Q = m·c·ΔT with c = 4.18 kJ/kg·K
Comment on why real systems add a margin and use a thermostat and bypass

bank.q: A supercharger raises intake pressure from 1.0 bar to 1.6 bar absolute from 300 K. Treating compression as isentropic with γ = 1.4, find the delivery temperature and the density ratio.
outline: Density ratio = (p₂/p₁)(T₁/T₂) = 1.6 × 300/343 ≈ 1.40
So about 40% more air mass per cycle if volumetric efficiency stays the same
Note that real compression is not isentropic and a compressor efficiency of 0.7–0.8 must be used

bank.q: An intercooler cools the compressor delivery from 343 K to 313 K at almost constant pressure. Find the percentage rise in air density and explain the effect on engine power.
outline: At constant pressure, density ratio = T₂/T₃ = 343/313 = 1.096
About 9.6% more air mass in the same volume
With the same air–fuel ratio, about 9.6% more fuel can be burnt, so roughly the same rise in power
Also lower intake temperature reduces knock tendency, allowing a higher compression ratio or more boost
Note the pressure drop across the intercooler and its effectiveness

bank.q: Explain turbo lag, its causes and the methods used to reduce it. Include variable geometry and intercooling in your answer.
outline: Cause: turbo speed depends on exhaust energy, which depends on fuel burnt; time constant of rotor inertia and gas build-up
Worse at low engine speed and after a gearshift; worse with a large turbo chosen for peak power
Remedies: small turbo, twin-scroll and divided turbine housing, lightweight compressor and turbine wheels, ball bearings, blow-off and wastegate control, VGT
VGT: vanes close at low flow to raise gas velocity and turbine work, open at high flow to avoid over-boost
Intercooling does not cut lag but raises the density benefit of the boost that does arrive

bank.q: Compare supercharging and turbocharging. Discuss the effects of supercharging on engine power, knock, thermal loading and the modifications needed in the engine.
outline: Drive: mechanical (belt/gear) versus exhaust turbine; parasitic loss versus waste energy recovery
Response: immediate versus lag; boost curve against engine speed
Effect on power: power roughly proportional to air mass flow; volumetric efficiency and trapping efficiency change
Knock: higher intake temperature and pressure raise knock in SI engines; intercooling and retarded timing or lower compression ratio used
Thermal loading: higher gas temperature and pressure, hotter exhaust valve and piston; need for richer mixture at full load to cool the charge
Modifications: lower compression ratio, stronger pistons, connecting rods and bearings, better cooling and lubrication, sodium-cooled or better valve material, intercooler, boost control

bank.q: Compare cross-flow, loop and uniflow scavenging in two-stroke engines. Which gives the best scavenging efficiency and why?
outline: Cross: transfer and exhaust ports opposite, charge short-circuits to exhaust, poor scavenging efficiency, but simple
Loop (Schnürle): transfer ports angled to loop the charge up the back wall and over the head, pushing burnt gas out, used in most small petrol two-strokes
Uniflow: inlet ports at one end and exhaust valves or ports at the other, charge moves in one direction; best scavenging, needs a valve or opposed pistons
Compare scavenging efficiency, charging efficiency, charge loss and specific output
Also mention crankcase-scavenged versus blower-scavenged and the effect of exhaust tuning

bank.q: A small turbocharged petrol car is used mostly in stop-and-go Indian city traffic. Discuss the cooling, lubricant and boost-control choices you would make and why.
outline: Cooling: pressurised forced circulation with thermostat, electric fan that runs after shutdown to protect the turbo bearing, coolant with glycol and corrosion inhibitors
Lubrication: fully synthetic or semi-synthetic multigrade with high viscosity index, anti-wear and anti-oxidant additives, oil-cooled turbo bearing, short oil change interval for short trips
Turbo protection: idling before shutdown, oil feed from the main gallery with a restrictor and drain to the sump
Boost control: small turbo or VGT for early boost, intercooler to reduce knock at high ambient temperature, wastegate or electronic boost control
Trade-offs: fuel quality and knock, cost of synthetic oil against turbo life, heat soak in traffic

glossary.def: An account of where the chemical energy of the fuel goes: brake power, coolant, exhaust, friction and radiation.
A thin extended metal surface on an air-cooled engine that increases the area available for convection to air.
The set of cast passages in the block and head through which liquid coolant flows around hot parts.
A tube-and-fin heat exchanger that transfers heat from the coolant to the air stream.
A temperature-operated valve that keeps coolant away from the radiator until the engine reaches its working temperature.
Coolant circulation driven only by the density difference between hot and cold coolant, with no pump.
Coolant circulation produced by a pump, so the flow rate is set by pump speed and not by temperature alone.
The liquid used in a cooling system, normally water with ethylene glycol and corrosion inhibitors.
The internal resistance of a fluid to flow, quoted in centistokes (cSt) at a stated temperature or as an SAE grade.
A scale showing how much an oil's viscosity falls as temperature rises; higher index means less change.
The lowest temperature at which the oil will still flow under standard test conditions.
The temperature at which oil vapour gives a momentary flash when a flame is applied; a low value warns of fuel dilution.
A chemical blended into a base oil to give a property the base oil lacks, such as anti-wear or detergency.
A lubrication layout in which the oil supply sits in a pan under the crankshaft and drains back to it by gravity.
A lubrication layout in which oil is scavenged to a separate tank and pumped back under pressure to the engine.
Lubrication of small two-strokes by oil premixed with fuel, with no pump, filter or sump.
The difference between indicated power and brake power, spent on rubbing contacts and on driving auxiliaries.
The ratio of brake power to indicated power, η_mech = BP/IP.
A mechanically driven compressor that raises the pressure and density of the air entering the engine.
A turbine–compressor pair on a common shaft, where exhaust gas drives the turbine and the compressor boosts intake air.
The delay between a demand for power and the delivery of boost, set by rotor inertia and the time needed to build exhaust energy.
A heat exchanger that cools air leaving the compressor before it enters the intake manifold.
A turbocharger whose turbine inlet vanes move to match gas flow, giving high boost at low speed and safe boost at high speed.
The removal of burnt gas from a two-stroke cylinder and its replacement by fresh charge during the port overlap.
The first rush of high-pressure burnt gas out of the exhaust port when it opens, before fresh charge arrives.
The amount by which intake pressure exceeds atmospheric pressure, usually quoted in bar.
